Q: How to autogenerate API documentation from Express route mappings? A:

This question is ancient, but I landed here while dealing with the same thing last month, so I figured I’d drop an updated answer for anyone still running into this.

The old monkey‑patching tricks and res.app._router.map stopped being reliable a few Express versions ago. Nowadays I’d approach this one of three ways, depending on how much control you want.

1. Swagger / OpenAPI with annotations (most common)
If you’re willing to add a few JSDoc‑style comments above your routes, swagger-jsdoc and swagger-ui-express will generate a full interactive API doc for you. It’s the standard for a reason — clients and front‑end devs already know how to read it.

2. express-routes-catalogue or similar lightweight parsers
Packages like express-routes-catalogue can scan a modern Express 4/5 app and spit out a JSON tree of all your routes. You then feed that tree into a simple Markdown template and you get a readable README without touching every handler. Not as pretty as Swagger, but zero‑annotation.

3. AI Code Documentation Generator (something I’m working on)
I got tired of tweaking templates, so I ended up building an API that takes raw route definitions (or any code snippet) and returns a clean Markdown doc. It auto‑detects the language, so it understands Express code out of the box, and it can output in 13 languages if you ever need localized docs.
Disclaimer: I’m the maintainer of this API.

The first two options are completely free. The API has a free tier (50 req/month) and the code is open source if you want to see how it works or self‑host:
https://github.com/zhaochangbo888/docgen-api

All three are solid. If you just need a quick, human‑readable README without writing a single annotation, option 3 saves me a ton of time these days. Hope that helps somebody who stumbles on this old question.

Q: Playwright python script function waiting at book 161 A:

After you've gone back a bunch of times with page.go_back(), the thumbnails locator gets totally out of sync with what's actually on the page. When you hit thumbnails.nth(i), it's basically pointing at the wrong thumbnail, which kicks off an endless retry loop that grinds everything to a halt around book 161 , that's like 8 pages worth of DOM chaos stacked up. The thing is, playwright locators are pretty smart about refreshing stale references - but they only do it if the element itself goes bad. When you navigate around and the whole DOM structure shifts, the locator doesn't know it needs to rebuild that nth-index map. So over time, the index stops matching reality, and - infinite retries that freeze your whole script.

So basically, you gotta refresh that locator every time you call go_back() so it actually knows what's up with the DOM.

await thumbnail.click()

await page.go_back()

await page.wait_for_selector("".product_pod"")

thumbnails = page.locator("".thumbnail"")

Throw your loop into a try-except block with some hard timeouts so you can bail out early if the retries start spiraling. This way, thumbnails.nth(i) always grabs the right thumbnail from whatever the page looks like rn, not some stale memory of what it used to look like. Kills the whole stacking up misalignment problem before it kills your script

Q: GitHub Action not triggering on push A:

There must be something else wrong - all you have here in this workflows is just fine.

You can see it working here: https://github.com/grzegorzkrukowski/stackoverflow_tests/actions/runs/1860382530

For this commit: https://github.com/grzegorzkrukowski/stackoverflow_tests/commit/f3f8dd20fa780746441c7b6623b6a2a9929aa70d

It's exact copy of workflow from your question.

I would expect you are pushing a file with different name - keep in mind some systems will be case-sensitive - so pushing data/sales.csv won't work properly. Another idea is that you pushing it to wrong branch or you have wrong path to the file. You have to push to test branch and with data/Sales.csv - it only triggers workflow if both are true.

Short answers is - workflow is fine as it is - no brackets needed. I could help more seeing the repository with this workflow and exact commits being done.

Q: sgslufread: Hard error on read, OS error = 104 Linux A:

Oracle Internet Directory (OID) ldapbind gives: sgslufread: Hard error on read, OS error = 10054 We were using a Cisco Load Balancing Router (LBR or CSS) and trying to do a simple ldapbind -p 389 -h machine would give the following error: sgslufread: Hard error on read, OS error = 10054 (on windows) sgslufread: Hard error on read, OS error = 104 (on linux) ldap_bind: Can't contact LDAP server

(might have also seen sgslufread: Hard error on read, OS error = 194 )

It turned out that the LBR was configured with Layer 5 load balancing (it does URL inspection). It is turned on by adding url "/" to the content content layer5 protocol tcp vip address xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx add service server1 port 389 url "/" active

The problem is that we have LDAP traffic, not HTTP traffic. Layer5 (url "/") is for HTTP traffic. Removing the url "/" took care of the issue.

I also received the same error when using an F5 load balancer to connect via LDAPS (SSL encrypted) on port 636. In this case the solution was to turn off the F5 LDAP monitor for port 636. For some reason the F5 does not like to monitor the OID SSL LDAP port.

Q: Spring Batch with SQL Server: Best approach for full-file aggregation before processing 4M records — memory vs performance vs lock contention A:

I'd recommend the staging table + SQL aggregation approach. SQL Server is built for grouping and deduplication, so it's more scalable and avoids large heap usage. In Spring Batch, use DataSourceTransactionManager with small batch commits, and fix the idle connection issue with connection pool/keepalive settings instead of changing the transaction manager.
